analysis.one_liner: Strips the EPA's power to overrule state decisions on water pollution permits and standards.
analysis.headline: The bill received no committee or floor vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013, leaving the EPA's clean-water override authority intact.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Clean Water Act so the EPA could no longer step in when it disagreed with a state's water quality standard or a state-issued pollution discharge permit. It also would have limited the EPA's power to block using waterways and wetlands as disposal sites for dredged or fill material unless the state agreed, and it shortened the deadlines agencies have to comment on permit applications. It added requirements that the EPA analyze and publicize the job and economic effects of its water rules, state by state, and hold hearings where more than 100 jobs could be lost, while requiring an annual report on toxic pollutants in state-regulated waters.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that discharge pollutants into rivers and streams — mining companies, manufacturers, and utilities — because a state permit or state water standard would become essentially final, with the EPA unable to veto it. States would also gain final authority over water decisions within their borders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Polluting industries and state permit holders

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the EPA from issuing a new or stricter water quality standard for a pollutant when it has already approved the state's standard, unless the state agrees the change is necessary.

Bars the EPA from overriding a state's determination that a discharge complies with pollution limits, and from objecting to or withdrawing approval of a state-issued discharge permit simply because it disagrees with the state's interpretation of the standard.

Restricts the EPA's power to deny or restrict using an area as a disposal site for dredged or fill material unless the state where the discharge originates concurs that the discharge would cause unacceptable harm.
Cuts the window for federal agencies to comment on dredge-and-fill permit applications from 90 days to 30 (or 60 if more time is requested), speeding up permitting decisions.

Requires the EPA to analyze the employment and economic effects of its water rules state by state, post the analysis publicly, notify affected officials, and hold hearings in any state expected to lose more than 100 jobs or $1 million in economic activity.
Requires an annual EPA report to Congress on changes in waterborne pathogens, toxic chemicals, and toxic metals such as lead and mercury in state-regulated waters.

analysis.who_pays: Communities whose rivers, streams, and drinking-water sources could be degraded when a state approves weak standards or permits — including downstream neighbors of upstream polluters, who would have no federal check to appeal to.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities relying on federal water-quality backstops

drawbacks.text: Eliminates the federal backstop in the Clean Water Act: if a state adopts weak water quality standards or issues weak permits, the EPA could not correct it, and pollution would not stop at the state line — downstream states would bear the cost of upstream decisions they cannot control.

The required job-loss analysis counts only gross losses and expressly forbids counting offsetting job gains from new technologies, so it would overstate the economic cost of cleaner-water protections and ignore the health benefits of reduced pollution.

Cutting agency comment deadlines on fill permits from 90 days to 30 gives federal wildlife and environmental reviewers far less time to assess harm to fish, shellfish beds, and drinking-water supplies before a permit is issued.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's concrete benefits go almost entirely to industries seeking permits — they would face no federal veto of state approvals and faster permit reviews. States would gain real authority, and the jobs analysis and public hearings would give affected communities a formal voice when EPA rules hit local economies. But those gains are offset by a real weakening of water protection: the EPA's authority to correct a state's weak standard, veto a bad permit, or block filling a waterway would be gone or conditional on state consent. The annual toxic-pollutant report is transparency after the fact, not protection. On balance, the bill traded a public safeguard for industry and state permitting convenience.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in September 2012, near the end of the session, and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up; it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia, joined by Republican Senator Pat Toomey, introduced the bill on September 19, 2012, describing it as a measure to preserve each state's authority over water quality determinations.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day it was introduced.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup and the Senate never voted on the bill before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
The bill arrived in the final months of a two-year Congress with only one cosponsor, leaving no realistic window for committee work or floor time.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the EPA's authority to override state water decisions and veto harmful permits was left untouched — an outcome that preserves the status quo for people who depend on that federal backstop for clean water, rather than for the permit-seeking industries the bill would have shielded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The EPA's clean-water backstop stayed intact.

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to preserve state authority over water quality standards and permits.

for.name: Sen. Pat Toomey
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred; the committee never held a markup or vote on it, and it died there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Democrat and a Republican — but it never reached a vote, so there is no record of how either party would have lined up.

industries.industry: Coal mining, including mountaintop removal in Appalachia
industries.note: The bill would bar the EPA from overriding a state's permit decisions or blocking waterways as fill disposal sites unless the state agrees — the very federal tools used against large Appalachian mine permits and related water guidance, and the sponsor's home state had high-profile disputes with the EPA over mine permitting. The industry's gain in cheaper permitting comes directly at the cost of federal oversight of the streams those operations fill and degrade.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and utilities holding discharge permits
industries.note: Once a state determines a discharge complies with pollution limits or issues a permit, the EPA could not veto it even if it disagreed with how the state interpreted the standard. That removes the federal check that protects downstream communities from weak state oversight.

industries.industry: Developers and infrastructure builders seeking dredge-and-fill permits
industries.note: They would gain from shorter federal review deadlines (30 days instead of 90) and from needing state concurrence before the EPA can block a disposal site. The bill, however, expressly preserves the EPA's authority to regulate pipelines that cross streambeds, so the gain is not total.

States would get the final word on standards, permits, and fill-disposal decisions, and the bill allows states to run part of the federal dredge-and-fill permit program. That is genuine sovereignty, but it shifts the cost of weak state decisions onto downstream states and residents.
